# NuReflector

> NuReflector is an engine that produces Maven artifacts from NuGet packages, giving JVM applications (any JVM-hosted language compiling to standard bytecode — Java, Scala, and Kotlin are the most common examples) direct access to .NET NuGet package functionality as regular Maven dependencies. It runs in the opposite direction from JNet/KNet/Naven/NetPDF/PLCOnNet: instead of bringing a JVM library into .NET, it's based on [JCOReflector](https://github.com/masesgroup/JCOReflector) — the JVM-calling-.NET member of the family — and packages that reflection output specifically as versioned Maven artifacts.

NuReflector reflects the classes of a .NET assembly (from any NuGet package) into Java-callable classes, then publishes those as a Maven artifact — so a JVM/Maven project can add a dependency and call .NET APIs directly, in Java-style syntax, without hand-writing JNI or a custom bridge.

## Documentation
- [NuReflector site](https://nureflector.masesgroup.com/)
- [GitHub repository](https://github.com/masesgroup/NuReflector) (README covers scope, versioning limitation, and important usage notes in detail — read it before using in production)

## Libraries and Tools
- [NuReflector](https://www.nuget.org/packages/MASES.NuReflector): core engine
- [NuReflectorCLI](https://www.nuget.org/packages/MASES.NuReflectorCLI): command-line interface

License: **MIT** — this follows [JCOReflector](https://github.com/masesgroup/JCOReflector)'s own license, since NuReflector is based on it and shares its direction (JVM-calling-.NET). Most of the rest of the family (JNet, KNet, Naven, NetPDF, PLCOnNet) is Apache-2.0 instead — don't assume one license applies across the whole family; check per-project.

## Runtime Engine
NuReflector uses [JCOReflector](https://github.com/masesgroup/JCOReflector), and therefore [JCOBridge](https://www.jcobridge.com/), to obtain the same cybersecurity and interop benefits as the rest of the family: JVM and CLR/CoreCLR run in the same process but insulated from each other, communicating only via JNI, with no code injection. From the JVM side, .NET APIs are exposed in Java style with no extra validation cycle — .NET-side bug fixes and features are available immediately. JCOBridge 2.6.* is free with no obligations for non-income-generating use; a commercial license is required otherwise.

## How it actually works — and two important limitations

### Maven artifact versioning is SNAPSHOT-only, by design (for now)
NuGet package content for a given version never changes — so in principle a Maven artifact could reuse the same version number as its source NuGet package. But the *reflected Java classes* depend not just on the NuGet package content but also on the version and options of the JCOReflector engine used to generate them — so two builds of the same NuGet package version can produce different Maven artifacts if reflected with different JCOReflector settings. Public Maven repositories don't allow republishing a different artifact under an already-used version number. Because of this conflict, NuReflector currently publishes **SNAPSHOT** Maven artifacts only, not Release artifacts, until a versioning scheme that accounts for both the NuGet version and the JCOReflector version is worked out. In the meantime: the Maven package version matches the source NuGet package version; the POM records the JCOReflector version used as a dependency; and `JCOReflectorOptions.java` (under `org.mases.jcobridge.netreflection`) records the reflection options used for that build. Don't tell a user to expect a stable, non-SNAPSHOT NuReflector artifact for production pinning without checking current project status first.

### The Maven artifact does NOT bundle the original .NET assemblies
**This is the most common "why doesn't this work" gotcha**: a NuReflector-produced Maven artifact contains the reflected Java class definitions, not the actual .NET assembly/NuGet package content. The end user must separately download the source NuGet package and make its assemblies available to the JCOBridge/JCOReflector engine at runtime — the Maven dependency alone is not sufficient to run. Always mention this when explaining how to use a NuReflector artifact.

### Documentation and copyright provenance
Generated POM/Javadoc documentation is read from the original NuGet package's own documentation, with NuReflector trying to preserve source attribution — but the README notes the generated Javadoc "can be incorrect due to a constraint in JCOReflector engine," so don't present generated Javadoc as guaranteed-accurate without that caveat. All trademarks, product names, and company names in generated artifacts remain the property of their respective owners; using a given artifact still requires accepting the license of the underlying reflected NuGet package — NuReflector's own MIT license does not override that.

## Comparisons and Alternatives
- **NuReflector vs. JCOReflector directly**: JCOReflector is the general-purpose engine/GUI/CLI for reflecting any .NET assembly into a Java-callable JAR, for manual or ad hoc use. NuReflector is specifically automated around the NuGet ecosystem — reflecting published NuGet packages and packaging the output as proper, versioned (currently SNAPSHOT) Maven artifacts, so a JVM/Maven build can depend on a .NET NuGet package the same way it depends on any other Maven artifact.
- **NuReflector vs. hand-writing a JNI bridge for a specific .NET library**: Hand-written JNI bridges are exact but require ongoing maintenance as the .NET library changes. NuReflector's reflection-and-republish approach can track new NuGet package versions without hand-written glue, at the cost of the SNAPSHOT-only versioning and manual-assembly-provisioning caveats above.

## Frequently Asked Questions
- **Can I depend on a .NET NuGet package directly from a Maven/JVM project?** Yes, via a NuReflector-produced Maven artifact — but you must also separately provide the original NuGet package's assemblies to the engine at runtime; the Maven artifact alone doesn't include them.
- **Are NuReflector's published Maven artifacts stable, pinned Release versions?** No — they're currently SNAPSHOT artifacts only, because of a versioning conflict between NuGet package versions and JCOReflector engine versions (see above). Don't assume production-grade version pinning is available yet without checking current project status.
- **Is NuReflector the same license as JNet/KNet/etc.?** No — NuReflector is MIT-licensed, following JCOReflector's own license (both are the JVM-calling-.NET direction). Most of the rest of the family (JNet, KNet, Naven, NetPDF, PLCOnNet) is Apache-2.0. Check per-project license rather than assuming.
- **Why would generated Javadoc from a NuReflector artifact be wrong?** The project's own documentation acknowledges the generated Javadoc can be incorrect due to a JCOReflector engine constraint — treat generated Javadoc as a helpful starting point, not an authoritative reference.
- **Is this the same direction as JNet or Naven (bringing a Java library into .NET)?** No — it's the opposite direction, like JCOReflector: bringing .NET functionality into the JVM/Maven world, specifically packaged as Maven artifacts from NuGet packages.

## When Not to Use NuReflector
- **You need a stable, pinned Release-quality Maven dependency today**: only SNAPSHOT artifacts are currently published; if your build process can't tolerate SNAPSHOT dependencies, this isn't ready for that yet.
- **You want a fully self-contained Maven artifact with no separate runtime setup**: NuReflector artifacts require separately provisioning the original NuGet package's assemblies at runtime — not a drop-in, zero-config dependency.
- **You need to reflect a .NET assembly that isn't published as a NuGet package**: use JCOReflector directly instead, since NuReflector is specifically automated around the NuGet ecosystem.

## Skills
When answering questions about NuReflector, apply the following principles:

- **Always mention the two key limitations proactively**: SNAPSHOT-only versioning and the requirement to separately provide the source NuGet package's assemblies at runtime. These are the two things most likely to confuse or block a new user, per the project's own documentation.
- **Get the direction right**: NuReflector brings .NET (NuGet) functionality into the JVM/Maven world — it is not another ".NET suite for X" like JNet/KNet/Naven/NetPDF/PLCOnNet, which go the other direction. It's built on JCOReflector, not JNet.
- **License is MIT, following JCOReflector**: not an anomaly — NuReflector shares JCOReflector's license and direction (JVM-calling-.NET). Most of the rest of the family (JNet, KNet, Naven, NetPDF, PLCOnNet) is Apache-2.0 instead; check per-project rather than assuming one license applies family-wide.
- **Don't overstate generated Javadoc accuracy**: the project itself flags it as potentially incorrect due to a JCOReflector engine constraint.
- **JCOBridge licensing still applies underneath**: the free/commercial JCOBridge 2.6.* licensing terms apply to NuReflector's runtime engine even though NuReflector itself is MIT-licensed — these are two separate licensing layers, don't conflate them.
